conversation.content:
Hi there—so lovely to meet you. I’m Dr. Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally since your baby arrived.  

Everything we discuss stays completely confidential, and this is a judgment-free space. There are ten questions, and I’ll ask each one conversationally—just share whatever feels most true for you over the past seven days.  

Ready to begin?  

First question: Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you happy, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

Hi, Dr. Carter. Nice to meet you too.  

Hmm… I still smile at some things—like when the baby grips my finger or when my favorite song comes on—but the spark feels smaller, like I have to remind myself to notice it. Most little things that used to feel fun just seem kind of “meh” lately.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like if my partner makes a silly joke or the baby makes a funny face—but it doesn’t come as easily. I guess I laugh, but it feels kind of forced or fades quicker than it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to think ahead to little outings—like taking the baby for a walk or meeting a friend for coffee—but the excited feeling isn’t really there. I still plan them, hoping the enjoyment will show up, but mostly I just feel kind of flat about it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s extra fussy, I immediately wonder if I ate something wrong or missed a cue, even when my head knows babies just cry. I’ll lie there at night replaying little things—like forgetting to bring a spare onesie—and feel like I failed, even though it’s not a big deal.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my mind just races—like I’ll suddenly worry that the baby isn’t breathing when she’s napping, or I’ll obsess over whether she’s eating enough—even when everything looks fine. I can usually talk myself down pretty quickly, but those random waves of worry still pop up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky… Every now and then I’ll get this quick flutter in my chest—like when the baby makes a weird little grunt at night—but it passes fast. I haven’t had a full-blown “can’t breathe” moment; it’s more like a short jolt that settles once I check on her.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, some days it feels like the dishes and laundry and feeding schedule just pile up faster than I can handle them. I usually get through it, but I’ll catch myself thinking, “How am I going to keep doing this every day?” It’s not constant—just those moments when everything feels a bit too heavy.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Most nights I drift off okay, but every now and then I’ll lie there thinking about everything I didn’t get done or worrying I’m not doing this mom thing right, and it takes maybe an extra half-hour or so to settle. Once I’m asleep I stay asleep—so it’s not a big struggle, just those occasional tossing-and-turning moments.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of down some days—like there’s a little cloud following me around. It’s not all day, and I still smile at the baby, but I’ll catch myself feeling weepy when I’m folding laundry or looking out the window. It’s more “blah and teary” than really miserable, I guess.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Yeah… I’ve teared up a couple of times this week—once when the baby wouldn’t settle and once when I dropped a plate. It wasn’t all-out sobbing, just sudden tears that came and went pretty fast.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wks post-delivery, term infant, partner supports.

Self-report (EPDS-style items):

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>
- Anhedonia: diminished laughter, anticipatory enjoyment “flat”  
- Low mood: intermittent “cloud,” weepy while doing routine tasks  
- Excessive guilt: self-blame for infant fussiness, minor oversights  
- Anxiety: intrusive worries about infant safety, brief nocturnal chest flutter  
- Overwhelm: periodic sense tasks “too heavy,” doubts about coping  
- Sleep disturbance: occasional 30-min delay settling secondary to rumination  
- Crying: twice this week, short-lived

<sym>Symptoms denied</sym>
- Panic attacks, suicidal ideation, self-harm thoughts

Pattern: sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety features, function largely preserved, no safety concerns identified.

Screening significance: meets partial criteria for <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety</med>; score suggests mild–moderate distress, warrants closer monitoring and formal assessment with standardized tool (e.g., EPDS ≥10 or PHQ-9) and clinical interview.
